Added 2 new regression tests (ghost/never-existed and deactivated) proving the unassign now succeeds. Also had to CORRECT the setup of 2 PRE-EXISTING tests (REST 'removing the fleet's last remaining Administrator grant is refused 409' and its MCP twin): both seeded 'soleadmin' as a GHOST admin (a principal_roles row with no matching auth.users row at all) and asserted a 409 refusal -- they were passing only because of this exact bug (a ghost-only store's count was already 0, so the pre-fix code spuriously refused removing the ghost too). Post-fix, that scenario correctly SUCCEEDS, so both tests were amended to seed an ACTIVE auth.users row for 'soleadmin', making them genuine last-real-administrator tests. This is corroborating evidence the finding was real, not merely a hypothetical edge case: 2 pre-existing tests in the tree were unknowingly asserting the buggy behavior.
classification_rationale: the guard's actual delete-then-recount logic did not match its own documented intent (refuse only when the delete itself removed a counted admin) -- a truth mismatch between the code's behavior and its stated invariant, forced into this enum's closest fit for a pure logic defect

trigger: test_rbac_store.cpp used a blind sleep_for(500ms) at 3 sites to 'prove a thread has started' before proceeding, instead of polling for a genuine Postgres lock wait -- CLAUDE.md forbids sleep_for+assume-timing synchronization
summary: Replaced all 3 sites with a shared poll_for_blocked_backend_pid() helper polling pg_stat_activity for wait_event_type='Lock'. Provenance is MIXED, not uniformly new: the CHAOS-1 site's blind sleep_for(500) predates A2 (a pre-existing #2703-era test); the other 2 sites (the A2 last-Administrator-guard concurrency tests) are genuinely new to this PR. Non-trivial discovery during the fix: the helper MUST run on a SEPARATE ad-hoc connection, never the lock holder's own connection -- PostgreSQL snapshots pg_stat_activity ONCE per transaction, so probing through the holder's already-open explicit-BEGIN transaction re-reads a frozen pre-block snapshot forever (verified empirically via live psql + pg_backend_pid self-queries; the ORIGINAL C2 test's blind sleep_for(500) was, in hindsight, load-bearing for snapshot freshness, not timing -- correct by accident). Documented this in the helper's own doc comment so a future reader does not simplify it back to the holder's connection.
classification_rationale: the test's actual synchronization technique (blind sleep_for) contradicted CLAUDE.md's own documented, hook-enforced convention against sleep_for+assume-timing -- forced into this enum's closest fit

trigger: is_rbac_administrator() (rbac_admin_predicate.hpp) gates POST/DELETE /api/v1/rbac/roles/{name}/assignments and never consulted session.mcp_tier, unlike every other admin-only route (AuthRoutes::require_admin denies ANY non-empty mcp_tier outright). An MCP bearer token minted at ANY tier (even the least-privileged 'readonly') for a principal who separately holds durable Administrator authority, presented to the REST route instead of the MCP tool, reached kAdmin with no MFA step-up (mfa_step_up.cpp unconditionally exempts mcp_token/api_token sessions) and no maker-checker approval ticket (MCP-only machinery, REST has no equivalent) -- empirically reproducible: the PR's own RbacRoleHarness test fixture unknowingly exercised this by handing every REST session a non-empty mcp_tier (default 'supervised'). The predicate's own header doc comment (decision 3) falsely claimed parity with require_admin's posture.
summary: Added a required (no-default) RbacAdminSurface{kRest,kMcp} parameter to is_rbac_administrator(): kRest structurally denies any non-empty session.mcp_tier (mirroring require_admin's posture and the platform's #520 rule), kMcp applies no tier rule (the MCP transport's own tier_allows/requires_approval/#4309 empty-tier-deny ladder already fully governs it). Updated both REST call sites (rest_api_v1.cpp, passing kRest) and both MCP call sites (mcp_server.cpp, passing kMcp). Added a dedicated deny_mcp_token_session REST helper (mirrors deny_engine_session) for audit-truth reasons -- the predicate's own shared denial-reason string would misleadingly read as 'not a durable admin' for a caller who actually IS one. Split test_rbac_role_assignment.cpp's RbacRoleHarness session builder so REST sessions default to an EMPTY mcp_tier (rest_session_mcp_tier) instead of sharing the MCP-transport's 'supervised' default (session_mcp_tier) -- the exact fixture bug that was unknowingly exercising this gap. Added direct predicate tests (kRest denies readonly/operator/supervised under both RBAC-off and RBAC-on; kMcp negative control still reaches kAdmin) and REST-harness tests (403, no store mutation, audit detail names 'MCP token', on both POST and DELETE).
classification_rationale: the predicate's own header doc comment (decision 3) claimed 'the same posture AuthRoutes::require_admin already carries... for every other admin-only route', which was false (require_admin denies any non-empty mcp_tier; this predicate did not) -- corrected in the same fix. Separately: the reviewer's own proposed remediation (an unconditional non-empty-mcp_tier deny inside the predicate) was evaluated and REJECTED, independently adjudicated by an enterprise-architect (Fable) agent who designed the accepted fix instead -- an unconditional deny would make assign_rbac_role/unassign_rbac_role permanently unreachable, since their own dispatch path deliberately gates a supervised-tier caller through to this SAME predicate after tier_allows/requires_approval's maker-checker ticket flow (verified: mcp_server.cpp ~line 21980/22164). The accepted fix is the surface-parameterized RbacAdminSurface design described in `summary` above.

trigger: unassign_role's last-Administrator guard captures locked_admin_principal_ids from a lock-time SELECT ... FOR UPDATE OF pr snapshot, but auth.users rows are deliberately never locked -- so a ghost/deactivated Administrator grant that is the fleet's ONLY Administrator at lock time can be reactivated by a fully independent, concurrent transaction (AuthDB::reactivate_user) in the gap between the lock query and the DELETE, and the stale snapshot alone lets the DELETE proceed unrefused, silently removing the last real admin's grant
summary: Fixed with a fresh, targeted post-DELETE re-check of auth.users.is_active for the specific deleted principal_id (only when it wasn't already in the lock-time snapshot), run in the same transaction immediately after the DELETE -- under READ COMMITTED this sees any reactivation that has ALREADY COMMITTED by that point, closing the race to a narrower, documented residual window (a reactivation committing strictly after the fresh check but before this transaction's own commit), matching this codebase's own accepted-staleness convention (#2703's bounded stale-serve precedent) rather than claiming the race fully closed. Deliberately does NOT lock auth.users (the explicitly-rejected alternative, per the guard's own 'never lock auth.users rows here' design note). Added a deterministic two-connection regression test (tests/unit/server/test_rbac_store.cpp) that seeds a ghost Administrator grant as the fleet's only admin, blocks the background unassign_role call on a test-only row lock (production's own FOR UPDATE OF pr lock query does not cover this row, since it's inactive at lock time -- a test-only synchronization device was needed), reactivates the account from a fully independent connection while the unassign is blocked, then confirms the unassign is now correctly REFUSED; also reconfirmed the pre-existing ghost-admin-succeeds test still passes (no regression to the original fix's own intent).
classification_rationale: the guard's stale lock-time snapshot did not match its own documented invariant (never leave the fleet with zero authenticatable administrators) under a specific, real interleaving -- same class as a2-up1's original 'guard does not actually hold' defect, on the same guard
